title: Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea
gist: Excerpt of a Foreign Affairs piece by Stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery arguing Trump is eager to restart summitry with Kim Jong Un (already scaling back joint drills with South Korea), but faces a far stronger North Korea than in 2019 — bolstered by nuclear/conventional expansion and Russian support — so his old concessions and tactics will no longer work.

themes.theme: Trump's push to restart Kim diplomacy

insights.claim: In an August 17 Truth Social post, Trump announced the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea, citing his 'very good relationship' with Kim Jong Un.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Reduced U.S.-ROK drills signals Washington is offering concessions up front, a potential concern for Seoul and regional defense posture.
insights.quote: The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”

insights.claim: Trump's eagerness to notch a foreign-policy win with North Korea is driven by legacy concerns and a stalemated war with Iran.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: A stalled Iran front raises odds of a headline-seeking Korea summit, which could move Korea-risk sentiment.
insights.quote: With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win.

insights.claim: Trump's two first-term summits with Kim aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula failed because the two sides had disparate expectations for the terms of a deal.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The core expectations gap remains unresolved, so a new summit carries high risk of another non-deal.
insights.quote: both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal

insights.claim: Kim Yo Jong denied knowledge of any current leader-level U.S.-North Korea communication while stressing that Kim Jong Un holds 'fond personal memories' of Trump, a signal the authors read as not closing the door to talks.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Pyongyang is keeping optionality and letting Washington court it, strengthening its bargaining leverage.
insights.quote: Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

insights.claim: North Korea has signaled not eagerness but at least an unwillingness to rule out renewed engagement, leaving the initiative with Pyongyang.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Timing of any summit is Pyongyang's call; watch North Korean statements for the trigger.
insights.quote: The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court

insights.claim: Unfinished first-term diplomacy, the COVID-19 pandemic, the sharp escalation of U.S.-China rivalry, and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement with North Korea.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: The structural backdrop for Korea diplomacy is worse than 2018-19, lowering odds of a substantive deal.

insights.claim: North Korea's continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and growing support from Moscow have strengthened Kim Jong Un's hand relative to 2019.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Russia-DPRK alignment reduces the effectiveness of U.S. pressure and sanctions; any deal likely tilts toward Pyongyang's terms.
insights.quote: North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand.

insights.claim: Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer rely on the concessions and negotiating tactics he used in previous talks, and personal rapport with Kim is unlikely to be enough to yield a deal.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of summit-driven 'peace dividend' narratives for Korean assets; a deal, if any, would require bigger U.S. concessions.
insights.quote: Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.
